analysis.one_liner: Lets investors subtract inflation from taxable gains on stocks, crypto, and property held over three years.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Ted Cruz with 7 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was filed and never received a vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let investors reduce their taxable capital gains by the amount of inflation on stocks, cryptocurrency, and business property held for more than three years, using the GDP price deflator. The same break would flow through mutual funds, ETFs, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, and similar entities. It applied only to assets bought after 2021. Introduced by Senator Ted Cruz with Republican cosponsors, it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large taxable investment portfolios — especially holders of individual stocks, digital assets like cryptocurrency, and business or rental property kept more than three years — plus the mutual funds, ETFs, REITs, and partnerships that channel those investments. Taxable capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, so most of the tax savings would go to the wealthiest taxpayers; assets in retirement accounts and homes covered by the main-residence exclusion would see little benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors with long-held taxable assets

how_it_helps.text: Investors could add measured inflation to the purchase price of stocks, digital assets, and tangible business property held more than three years, shrinking the taxable gain and the capital gains tax owed.
The same inflation adjustment would flow through mutual funds, ETFs, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, S corporations, and common trust funds to their individual investors.
The bill explicitly includes digital assets recorded on a distributed ledger — cryptocurrency and similar holdings — in the assets eligible for the inflation adjustment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, through lower capital gains tax revenue. The bill contains no offsetting tax increase or spending cut, so the lost revenue would be covered by borrowing or by other taxpayers over time. Because the benefit scales with the size of the gain, the direct savings would flow mainly to the highest-income households.

drawbacks.text: By lowering the tax on long-held investment gains, the bill would cut federal revenue with no offset; since taxable capital gains are concentrated among high-income households, most of the benefit would go to the top of the income distribution while the general budget absorbs the cost.
The relief would apply only to assets acquired after December 31, 2021 and held for more than three years, so it would not help families selling assets they bought earlier or held for a shorter time.

Indexing would add significant administrative complexity: taxpayers must document original purchase prices in writing, and the bill carries a web of special rules for short sales, related-party transfers, and pass-through entities, plus IRS authority to disallow transfers made mainly to game the adjustment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Indexing gains for inflation is a coherent fix for a real problem — taxing inflation as if it were income. Small savers holding taxable stocks or property for years would keep more of their true return. But the benefit scales with the size of the gain: taxable capital gains are concentrated among the wealthiest households, the bill has no offset for the lost revenue, and the most common family assets — homes with the main-residence exclusion and retirement accounts — would get little or nothing. On balance, the general budget would bear the cost while the gain would go disproportionately to the top.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended in January 2023, and the committee never voted on it.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on November 3, 2021, with six Republican colleagues named on the bill and a total of 7 Senate Republicans listed as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record — and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers are better off that a revenue-losing tax cut skewed toward the wealthiest households never became law; the wealthy investors and funds it targeted simply never received the break.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; wealthy investors got nothing

for.name: Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its promotion in the Senate.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All eight Republicans attached to the bill were sponsors or cosponsors and no Democrat signed on; because it never reached a vote, the full chamber's split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill explicitly extends inflation indexing to digital assets recorded on distributed ledgers, giving crypto investors a tax reduction on long-held holdings. The revenue cost falls on the general budget.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and ETFs (regulated investment companies)
industries.note: The bill writes detailed rules letting funds pass the inflation adjustment to shareholders, making taxable fund investing more attractive. The benefit accrues mainly to higher-income fund investors.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts and commercial property investors
industries.note: REIT stock and tangible business property are covered by the indexing rules, reducing tax on gains from long-held property. Ordinary renters and non-investors get no direct benefit from this.
The bill would reduce capital gains revenue with no offset, adding to deficits or forcing other taxes and cuts; ordinary taxpayers share that loss.
